concept.name: Overtrading
concept.definition: Trading more frequently or in greater aggregate volume than one's strategy, edge, or costs justify. Brokerage-account research by Barber and Odean shows individual investors' net returns decline with trading frequency, and the SEC-commissioned Library of Congress report lists active trading among the most damaging investor mistakes.
concept.intuition: Every trade pays the spread, fees, and slippage - if the edge per trade is thin or absent, more trades just means more cost and more noise.
concept.mechanics: Overconfidence and the desire for action push trade count beyond the arrival rate of valid setups; each marginal trade carries transaction costs and roughly zero or negative expectancy, so aggregate performance erodes with activity. Barber and Odean found the most active quintile of individual traders significantly underperformed the least active.
concept.failure_modes: Diagnosing overtrading requires knowing the strategy's true edge and cost structure; what looks like overtrading for one system is correct throughput for a genuine high-frequency edge. Boredom-driven or P&L-driven spikes in trade count are the practical signature.
concept.misconceptions: High activity is not inherently wrong - market makers and statistical arbitrageurs trade constantly with positive expectancy; overtrading means trading beyond one's validated edge, not merely trading a lot. Nor does more screen time create more opportunity.
concept.example: A swing trader whose backtest supports 40 trades a year takes 300, mostly marginal intraday punts; commissions and slippage consume the entire simulated edge.

citations.source: Behavioral Patterns and Pitfalls of U.S. Investors (Library of Congress, Federal Research Division, prepared for the U.S. SEC, August 2010)
